title: Markel ($MKL) 2026 Q2 update
content_html:
Dear Partners,

Markel reported its H1 ’26 figures. The full year and quarterly figures serve for us as a check on the essential KPIs that secure long-term value. Markel is a position for the decades, not for the next 90 days, as this table in the image shows us why:

"a system designed to relentlessly compound your capital"

Let’s get into it.

Insurance

The combined ratio came in at 92.9%. This means Markel recorded a profit on insurance and the combined ratio was lower than ratio in 2025, which had a combined ratio of 96.9 %:

“On the surface, reporting four quarters in a row of a low 90s combined ratio may appear a little boring. In that regard, long may boring continue.” – Simon Wilson, CEO Markel Insurance

The Insurance segment, responsible for the vast majority of revenue and operating result, reported an adjusted operating result of $376.5 Million, an increase of 40% compared to $269.8 million in Q2 2025:

The combined ratio of 92.9% is helped by $166.6 million of favorable reserve development (versus $78.9 million a year ago). This is normal and characteristic for Markel, whose reserving philosophy is “more likely redundant than deficient”. Consistent reserve releases are a sign of conservative underwriting :

The Insurance divisions

International. Gross premium volume grew 31% to $890.2 million, with a combined ratio of 82.0% . The interational division had a $41 million headwind from the middle east war. Growth in this division came from marine and energy, general liability, and professional liability lines. Simon Wilson’s former division is performing exceptionally well and is the driving force within the insurance sector in terms of growth and profitability

U.S. Wholesale and Specialty. Premiums fell 4% to $798.7 million, but this is by design, because management pulled back within general liability and property, rebalancing the mix toward more profitable business. The reward of focussing on profitability is that the combined ratio improved five points to 97.1%. As Wilson would say less volume, better quality “top line is vanity, bottom line is sanity” in practice.

“The improvement has come on the back of some tough decisions, where we have chosen the sanity of bottom-line profit over the vanity of top-line growth.” – Simon Wilson CEO Markel Insurance

One of the reasons to focus more on profitability in this division is mainly because competition increased and are taking more risks, risks that are unsustainable. Markel will not join these battles with competition as the situation could turn very quickly in the event of a catastrophe:

"The first half of this year, it's been very aggressive, the competition in that property segment. Given the results that have been announced thus far during the year, we can see people are making a lot of profit. Some of the reason for that is we haven't had the winds blow or the fires burn just yet." – Simon Wilson CEO Markel Insurance

“We are more in a defensive mode in that U.S. casualty market at the moment, and we are walking away from areas which are really causing the majority of losses to our book. We’ve probably accelerated that in the first half of this year.” – Simon Wilson CEO Markel Insurance

Programs and Solutions. The combined ratio here rose three points to 94.2%, driven by a higher attritional loss ratio (partly offset by favorable reserve development). This division is still absorbing the transition of the Hagerty business to a fronting arrangement, which lowers reported premium. Markel now collects a fronting fee instead of carrying the risk itself.

Global Reinsurance. The division placed into run-off last year posted a combined ratio of 123.6%, dragging the overall segment ratio down by two points. This is a known, temporary headwind, the book is winding down and will only fully leave the numbers over the next few years.

Growth in premiums written

A growth in premiums written (the total value of insurance policies a company sells in a given period) can directly lead to economies of scale in the insurance segment, which lower the expense ratio and support the combined ratio. The growth in Q2 looks weak, because net written premiums fell 6% to $2.04 billion, and on a gross underwriting basis the decline was even sharper at (15%). But this headline is misleading, and it is important to understand why.

The entire decline is the result of two deliberate structural decisions already discussed. The run-off of the Global Reinsurance division and the conversion of the Hagerty business to a fronting arrangement. Both are Markel walking away from risk it doesn't want anymore. That's a choice, not weakness.

Strip those two out and you see the real number. Markel’s own adjusted underwriting gross premium volume grew 10%. So the ongoing business isn't shrinking. It's growing 10%, and in the more profitable lines management wants to grow.

This growth matters for two reasons. 1) More premium spread over the same fixed cost base creates scale economies, which lower the expense ratio and support the combined ratio:

2) And just as important, an increase in premiums sold directly grows what is known as the ‘float’. The float represents the capital that the insurer, in this case Markel, can invest without incurring interest costs. It is the money Markel collects in premiums today but has not yet paid out in claims. It's basically an interest-free loan Markel can invest. A healthy, expanding, profitable premium base enlarges the pool of free investable capital, which compounds shareholder value over time. Growth for its own sake destroys value. Profitable growth, which is what we're seeing now, is what makes Markel work.

the State National write-down

State National runs a fronting business, it uses its licenses to write insurance on behalf of third-party capacity providers, fully passing the underwriting risk on to those partners in exchange for a fee. One of those capacity providers went bankrupt. Resulting in a $205 million bad-debt charge in the Financial segment, which pushed the segment to a $149 million loss on its own.

The relevant business that bankrupted began back in 2012, and Markel stopped writing these programs in 2021. Markel held collateral against this exposure, and as recently as year-end 2025 that collateral was adequate. But over the first half of 2026, after pulling more granular data and commissioning a third-party actuarial study, Markel substantially raised its estimate of the ultimate losses on these programs (mostly primary “habitational casualty” business). The losses grew faster than expected and ran past the collateral. Since Markel does not expect to recover the shortfall through additional collateral, it booked the $205 million as a provision for the uncollectible portion. As Gayner put it plainly:

“It’s the collateral’s fine, just that the losses... have moved at such a rate that it got ahead of the collateral.”

What I appreciate is the way management handled it. Gayner called this “the first substantial credit loss in State National’s over 40-year history” and framed it exactly as we would want:

“As is always the case at Markel, we do our best to recognize and report bad news quickly and let good news develop over time.”

One bad quarter doesn’t undo a great acquisition. It’s a real disappointment, but a one-off, not something structural. Markel bought State National in 2017 for roughly $900 million, and cumulative earnings from it since then are over $1 billion, even after absorbing this charge.

Ventures

The non-insurance businesses, which Markel groups under three segments, showed a mixed picture this quarter, with strong underlying performance in some areas masked by one-off items in others.

Industrial. Revenue rose 2% to $1.04 billion for the quarter (+4% for the half year), but adjusted operating income fell 27% to $75.4 million. Organic growth was essentially flat, and the revenue increase came largely from an acquisition made in December 2025. Higher demand for precast concrete and fire safety services in commercial construction was offset by weaker sales of car-hauling equipment (a cyclical downturn in that industry) and industrial bakery equipment. The profit decline reflects lower margins from a changed business mix and higher operating costs. Nothing structural here this looks cyclical.

Financial. On paper this segment collapsed into a loss of $148.9 million (versus a $78.4 million profit a year ago), but the headline is entirely explained by the $205.3 million credit-loss provision we discussed earlier, tied to a bankrupt capacity provider in State National’s fronting operations:

If you strip that out, the underlying picture is actually healthy. Organic revenue grew 6.4% in the first half, driven by higher management fees at Nephila (insurance-linked securities) and growth in lender services. The reported loss is a one-off, also not a sign of a structural broken business.

Consumer and Other. Revenue grew 4% to $552 million and adjusted operating income jumped 20% to $122.1 million:

The quarter benefits from seasonality (Costa Farms, the ornamental plant business and the segment’s largest, does most of its sales in Q2), helped by higher plant volumes and better margins, plus a full contribution from the EPI acquisition. Genuinely strong operational performance.

Taken together, Ventures remains what it has been for years. The quiet compounding jewel within the Markel Group. Quarter-to-quarter it will always be lumpy, with one-off items and cyclical swings, but the businesses keep generating cash that Markel can reinvest wherever it wants.

Investments

The income from the investment portfolio, consisting of dividends and interest, increased 11% to $256.1 million for the quarter (and 11% to $512 million for the half year). This is the recurring, stable engine of Markel’s investment operation, running at roughly $1 billion a year, and it is directly fed by the float we discussed in the insurance section.

Instead of a headwind from falling rates, the fixed-maturity yield rose to 3.7%. Markel is still reinvesting maturing bonds at rates above the portfolio’s average yield, and it is holding a larger bond portfolio than a year ago, so interest income on bonds climbed. Dividend income on equities also grew. The only drag came from lower yields on cash and short-term investments (2.8% versus 3.3%), a direct consequence of lower short-term rates.

Net investment gains of $1.17 billion for the quarter, almost entirely unrealized changes in the fair value of Markel’s equity portfolio, which returned 9.9% in the quarter. Readers of our Substack will remember that in Q1 2026 this same line was a large loss, with equities down 5.2%, and I urged patience, calling these swings noise. This quarter proves the point. The market recovered, the paper loss reversed, and over the first half the equity portfolio is back in positive territory. As of June 30, Markel’s equity portfolio sits on $9.3 billion of cumulative unrealized gains.

That's why we watch net investment income, not the mark-to-market swings. The quarterly fluctuations in equity value are meaningless in isolation, one reason being that the market often recovers before the next report is even out. What matters is that Gayner keeps compounding capital over the long term, which he's done for decades.

Capital allocation

For several quarters now, I have been asking the same thing. When will Markel finally fire up the buyback machine? This quarter, they delivered, but still they could be more aggresive. Markel repurchased $237 million of its own shares in the second quarter ($371 million year to date), at an average price of roughly $1,858 per share. Here's the allocation of recent quarters:

  • Q3 2025: $74 million

  • Q4 2025: $124 million

  • Q1 2026: $134 million

  • Q2 2026: $237 million

“At current prices and relative to the current set of alternatives, Markel shares represent the highest and best use of capital... we funded these repurchases through earnings. We are not leveraging up or borrowing money to repurchase shares.” – Gayner, CEO of Markel

That is a clear acceleration, nearly double the pace of the previous quarter. Here you can see the share repurchases over the previous years:

Markel is in the position of having the luxury of a 360-degree capital allocation framework. This essentially means that it can deploy capital to work at any time to where it can generate the best returns. The reason we place such emphasis on share buybacks is that we believe Markel’s intrinsic value is much higher than the value it has had today and in recent years.

Every share bought at prices below intrinsic value is highly accretive, it increases each remaining owner’s slice of the business at a discount. Over the past five years, Markel has reduced its share count by about 10% (from 13.7 million to 12.4 million shares), and Gayner has stated in last quarter (Q1 ’26) he expects to buy back the next 10% in less than five years at current prices. With $1.1 billion still available under the share repurchases program, there is plenty of room to keep going:

Conclusion Casteleyn Partnership

In recent years, Markel has been restructuring and streamlining its insurance division. The challenge with insurance is that it is a slow-moving business; this long-tail business takes years to run off the books completely. So today's figures still carry a few underperforming contracts that hide the real earning power. The Global Reinsurance division, which is being wound down in run-off; the long tail of an old State National programme that caused the credit loss this quarter and the accounting distortion resulting from Hagerty’s transition to a fronting model. None of this means the business is failing. It's the leftover of a company deliberately dropping risk it doesn't want.

This takes time, and when it finally happens, we will see what the reformed, Markel Insurance is truly capable of earning. That's why our long-term confidence in Markel only grows, right through the noise of one quarter As Gayner put it:

“The ability to make good long-term decisions and not be under unusual short-term quarterly pressure is really one of the keys and one of the factors that has allowed the double-digit compounding, the relentless compounding that’s been going on around here for decades.” - Tom Gayner

and we’re really looking forward to it.

Thank you for reading!

‘‘Patient capital. Driven by the discipline of learning.’’ - Casteleyn Partnership
